claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple single-phase solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength but high ductility and machinability.
The degree of local chemical short-range order governs the deformation behavior, hardness, and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
A rapidly quenched, homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has minimal short-range order.
Minimal short-range order permits relatively easy dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation glide causes low hardness and strength while retaining high ductility.
Annealing near 800 °C for 1–24 hours followed by controlled cooling can enhance short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid quenching after the thermal treatment retains a comparatively low degree of short-range order.
Local short-range order creates spatially diffuse energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Enhancing short-range order raises yield strength and hardness by increasing barriers to dislocation motion.
Excessive short-range order may reduce ductility and cause embrittlement.
Slow-cooled or extended-annealed specimens should have higher yield strength than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled or extended-annealed specimens should have higher hardness than rapidly quenched specimens.
The measured degree of short-range order should correlate with yield strength and hardness.
There should be a short-range-order threshold beyond which additional ordering reduces ductility.
The proposed ordering effects should occur without precipitation or grain-size refinement.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in compression at 25 °C and 600 °C after heat treatment near 800 °C for 1–24 hours.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant strength and hardness increase with enhanced short-range order would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a correlation between short-range order and mechanical-property changes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The loading range is restricted to the elastic–plastic transition or yield point, but the hypothesis also proposes measuring plastic strain at failure and identifying embrittlement. Failure strain and loss of ductility cannot be established if testing stops at yield.
